analysis.one_liner: Requires malpractice claims to go through arbitration-like panels before court, with fee penalties for contesting.
analysis.headline: A malpractice-overhaul bill with one sponsor and one cosponsor was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in November 2009 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed how medical malpractice cases work nationwide. Patients injured by malpractice would first have had to take their claim to an arbitration-like dispute resolution system — a state system the Attorney General certified, or a federal system in states without one. Only after that decision could they go to court, and only within 90 days. Anyone who contested the dispute resolution decision and did not end up with a better result would have had to pay the other side's court costs and attorneys' fees. A dispute decision nobody contested would carry the same legal force as a jury verdict. It would have applied to any doctor, nurse, hospital, or other provider where Medicare patients make up at least a quarter of the patient load, which covers most of the health care system.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers gain the most. Every malpractice claim would be channeled through a non-jury process first, claims would be decided within about 180 days of notice, and the fee penalty would make it financially risky for a patient to challenge a decision they lost. Malpractice payouts and litigation costs would likely fall, lowering providers' insurance premiums. The bill also required that findings of malpractice be reported to state disciplining agencies (unless the provider contested within 90 days), and some patients with clear-cut claims would have gotten a decision much faster than a court case typically takes.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any malpractice suit in state or federal court unless the claim has first been resolved by a certified dispute resolution system, with the court filing due within 90 days of that decision.
Requires a written decision within 180 days of the claim notice in most cases, which would be far faster than the years a malpractice trial often takes.

Mandates that any finding that a provider committed malpractice be transmitted to the state agency that monitors or disciplines health care providers, unless the provider contests the decision within 90 days.

Directs the Attorney General to certify state systems that meet federal requirements and to create a federal fallback system for states that do not have their own, so the pre-court process applies everywhere.
Directs the Comptroller General to study private litigation insurance markets, including whether 'loser pays' fee systems can still give ordinary people affordable access to the courts.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by malpractice. Under the bill's fee provision, a patient who contests the dispute resolution decision and does not end up with a more favorable court judgment must pay the provider's costs and attorneys' fees, unless a judge finds that would be manifestly unjust. That financial risk would push many patients with legitimate but hard-to-prove claims to accept the dispute resolution outcome rather than fight it. Plaintiffs' attorneys working on contingency would also face new financial exposure, and would take on fewer risky cases.

drawbacks.text: The fee penalty cuts both ways: a patient who challenges an unfavorable dispute resolution decision and wins no more in court must pay the provider's attorneys' fees, which could expose an injured patient to tens of thousands of dollars in costs and would deter many valid claims.

A dispute resolution decision that no party contests carries the same legal force as a jury verdict, so decisions made by a process that never involved a judge or jury become final judgments against patients who decline or cannot afford to fight them.

The bill preempts state court procedures for most malpractice claims, replacing each state's jury-trial process with a federally certified system for providers with 25% or more Medicare patients — effectively most of the health care system.

The bill's own text acknowledged an unresolved problem: it directed a study of whether 'loser pays' fee systems still provide ordinary people affordable access to courts, which supporters of the bill had not answered before imposing one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There are real trade-offs. Faster decisions and mandatory reporting of malpractice findings to state disciplining agencies would serve patient safety, and a patient with an airtight claim would likely get money sooner than in court. But the core mechanism shifts financial risk onto the injured patient: accept the non-jury decision, or fight it in court and pay the provider's lawyers if you do no better. Combined with binding uncontested decisions, the design is weighted toward resolving claims cheaply for providers and insurers rather than toward full compensation for injured patients, and the bill left open — by ordering a study — the very question of whether its fee system keeps courts affordable for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Lindsey Graham introduced the bill on November 2, 2009, joined by Sen. Saxby Chambliss as its sole cosponsor.
The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on the Judiciary; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed.

The bill would have required every malpractice claim against a covered provider to be initially resolved through an Attorney General-certified dispute resolution system before any lawsuit could be filed, with court filings due within 90 days of that decision.

Under the bill, a party that contested the dispute resolution decision and did no better in court would have owed the other side's costs and attorneys' fees, and an uncontested decision would have the same status as a court verdict.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by malpractice kept their existing right to take a claim before a judge and jury without first passing through a mandatory non-court process or risking a fee award. Doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers gained nothing, since the narrower, faster claim-resolution system they sought never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept court access

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 2, 2009, establishing mandatory pre-court dispute resolution for malpractice claims.

for.name: Sen. Saxby Chambliss
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; sole cosponsor

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral, leaving it without any committee action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the committee that buried it was run by Democrats.

industries.note: Mandatory pre-court resolution plus a fee penalty for contesting would shrink the number and size of claims that get paid, lowering insurer payouts. The insurer's gain comes directly out of what injured patients can recover.

Providers would face faster claim resolution and lower liability exposure, and would only have malpractice findings reported to disciplinary agencies if they failed to contest within 90 days. The bill's findings section frames malpractice litigation as a driver of high health costs and malpractice premiums, which providers would pass to patients.

A mandatory non-court step, a 90-day filing deadline, and fee exposure for losing a contest would cut the number of malpractice suits and raise the risk of taking contingency cases, so the attorneys who bring malpractice claims on behalf of patients would lose business.
